Abstract
This paper presents the architecture, performance characterization, and early sci-
entific impact of Toubkal, Africa’s most powerful supercomputer (TOP500 #356, 
Green500 #178 as of June 2025). Designed to support high-performance computing 
research across disciplines, Toubkal integrates CPU, high-memory, and GPU-accel-
erated nodes connected via a high-bandwidth InfiniBand fabric and powered in part 
by renewable energy sources. We benchmark Toubkal’s compute, memory, network, 
and storage subsystems using standard and reproducible tools (HPL, STREAM, 
IOR, OMB, HPL-MxP), reporting robust performance and energy-efficiency met-
rics. The CPU partition achieves 63% of its theoretical peak, while GPU-acceler-
ated HPL-MxP benchmarks on H100 nodes exceed 209 TFLOP/s per GPU. We also 
introduce a supervised learning model that predicts GPU frequency ranges minimiz-
ing the energy-delay product (EDP) across diverse workloads. The model achieves 
over 92% accuracy, with average gains of 13% in EDP, 13% in energy consumption, 
and a 1.1% reduction in kernel time across all kernels. The paper also compares 
Toubkal to several US DoE systems, analyzes early user growth, and documents 
real-world adoption across domains including AI, bioinformatics, and material sci-
ence. These results offer both a technical reference for reproducibility and a perfor-
mance baseline for emerging HPC centers worldwide. Beyond presenting a system 
deployment, this work contributes an early blueprint for sustainable, regional super-
computing infrastructure aligned with global standards.

1  Introduction
1.1  Motivation
The increasing complexity of scientific and technological challenges has driven 
global investment in high-performance computing (HPC) infrastructure. From 
weather forecasting and bioinformatics to materials science, quantum comput-
ing, and machine learning, modern research increasingly depends on large-scale 
computational resources. However, access to such infrastructure remains highly 
uneven. In Africa—home to over 1.4 billion people and facing critical issues in 
sectors such as agriculture, climate resilience, and health—computational capac-
ity is scarce. The continent hosts less than 1% of global data centers [1] and con-
tributes only 1% of international scientific output [2], a gap largely attributed to 
limited access to local resources.
This disparity coincides with a growing digital footprint. Mobile and fixed 
broadband usage has surged, generating substantial data volumes and increasing 
the demand for localized compute capabilities. Between 2019 and 2024, mobile 
Internet traffic in Africa rose from 3.9 to 23.2 exabytes—an approximately sixfold 
increase [3]—driven by over 230 million smartphone-based Internet users [1]. 
Yet, many African institutions continue to rely on expensive, remote digital ser-
vices or are altogether excluded from computational science. This infrastructural 
gap hinders scientific autonomy, exacerbates brain drain—with approximately 
70,000 skilled professionals lost annually [4]—and impedes sustainable develop-
ment across the region, which receives only 2% of global R&D investment [5].
To address these challenges, the Toubkal supercomputer was deployed in 2021 
at Mohammed VI Polytechnic University (UM6P) in Morocco. It is designed to 
provide robust, locally managed HPC services and currently represents the most 
powerful supercomputer in Africa. As of June 2025, it ranks ­356th on the TOP500 
list with a performance of 3.16 PFLOP/s and ­178th on the Green500 list with an 
energy efficiency of 4.18 GFLOPS/W. Toubkal consists of 1272 compute nodes, 
five high-memory nodes, and GPU partitions incorporating 20 A100 and 12 H100 
NVIDIA GPUs, interconnected via high-throughput InfiniBand and supported by 
8 PB of Lustre storage. It features an energy-efficient design that sets Toubkal 
apart from its regional and continental competitors. With an average power usage 
effectiveness (PUE) of 1.35, it leverages free cooling techniques and is comple-
mented by a 1 MWp on-site solar power plant, highlighting its commitment to 
sustainability and operational efficiency.
The system has already enabled research in diverse domains such as machine 
learning for weather forecasting, genomic selection for drought-resilient crops, 
and coastal hydrodynamics (see Sect. 2.5 for more details). Usage has grown rap-
idly, with active users doubling each year since 2023, including new participants 
from Sub-Saharan Africa and international institutions. These developments posi-
tion Toubkal as both a strategic asset for the region and a testbed for mid-scale 
HPC deployment in resource-constrained environments.

1.2  Research questions
This study aims to evaluate the technical performance, energy efficiency, and 
operational capabilities of Toubkal as a production-ready, mid-scale HPC system 
deployed within a resource-constrained regional environment. A central question 
we address is whether a supercomputer ranked ­356th globally can still deliver com-
petitive performance and energy efficiency when meticulously designed, optimized, 
and configured at both hardware and software levels. To explore this, we examine 
Toubkal’s performance across its compute, memory, storage, and network subsys-
tems using state-of-the-art benchmarking methodologies, providing a comprehen-
sive assessment of its capabilities, and ensuring that Toubkal after four years of its 
operation still achieves design-time performance of 3.16 PFLOP/s.
A secondary key research question we investigate is the potential for reducing 
GPU energy consumption through optimization techniques such as frequency scal-
ing. Specifically, we examine whether machine learning-based predictive models 
can effectively support workload-specific dynamic voltage and frequency scal-
ing (DVFS) optimization. This prompts us to assess the feasibility of ML-driven 
frequency range prediction, especially in the context of heterogeneous and mixed 
workloads, to enhance energy efficiency without compromising performance.
A third key research question in this paper addresses whether a mid-scale system 
like Toubkal can effectively support emerging scientific applications at scale, par-
ticularly those integrating AI and HPC. To this end, we examine practical workloads 
such as fine-tuning transformer-based large language models (LLMs) and conduct-
ing large-scale computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations, both of which have 
been successfully run on Toubkal. These real-world applications enable us to assess 
the system’s readiness to meet current HPC-AI convergence trends and its signifi-
cance for advancing regional scientific research.
Our final, fourth research question focuses on comparing Toubkal’s performance 
and energy efficiency to those of established US Department of Energy (DoE) sys-
tems. We evaluate how Toubkal stacks up against these larger, state-of-the-art plat-
forms and analyze early adoption metrics to assess its impact as a scientific com-
puting resource in underrepresented regions. This comparison aims to highlight 
Toubkal’s role in broadening access to high-performance computing and fostering 
scientific advancement in underserved areas.
1.3  Contributions
This paper presents the first comprehensive technical characterization of the Toubkal 
supercomputer, highlighting its hardware architecture, software environment, and 
deployment goals. In addressing the primary research question, we assess the sys-
tem’s performance and energy efficiency through standardized, reproducible bench-
mark suites that span compute, memory, storage, and networking subsystems. Our 
findings demonstrate that, thanks to continuous software updates and optimizations, 
Toubkal consistently meets its original design performance specifications.

To explore our second research question, we propose a workload-aware GPU 
DVFS strategy driven by supervised machine learning. A number of studies have 
explored GPU DVFS and energy-aware strategies in HPC contexts. In heterogene-
ous GPU clusters, Wang et al. [6] predict utilization and couple it with an energy 
model to avoid powering idle GPUs. In edge computing on heterogeneous multicore 
processors, Liu et al. [7] combine task prioritization, core-aware mapping, and pre-
dictive DVFS, cutting energy by 20.9% with only a 2.4% deadline-miss rate. Kocot 
[8] surveys energy-aware scheduling in HPC, including DVFS, power capping, and 
ML/fuzzy-logic policies. Mei et al. [9] show on NVIDIA Fermi and Maxwell that 
DVFS benefits depend on architecture and application behavior. Wang et al. [10] 
present DSO, a lightweight optimizer that fuses runtime metrics and static code fea-
tures with a "DVFS roofline" model, yielding about 19% energy-efficiency gains 
with < 5% performance loss. Kissami et  al. [11] benchmark H100 with cuBLAS 
and report workload- and precision-dependent efficiency; an ML-based frequency 
predictor outperforms standard governors. In contrast to these studies, our approach 
explicitly explores non-default frequency intervals to avoid relying on the GPU’s 
standard frequency settings. This allows us to identify workload-specific optimal 
ranges that are often overlooked by existing DVFS strategies. Our experimental 
results reveal that frequency tuning based on workload profiles can significantly 
lower energy consumption while maintaining near-optimal performance. In particu-
lar, memory-bound kernels such as memory copy operations benefit the most, with 
energy savings reaching up to 37.50%, and an overall average gain of 13.06% in 
energy and 13.13% in EDP, while also achieving a slight kernel time gain of 1.11% 
on average.
Furthermore, we analyze real-world usage patterns and active scientific projects, 
including fine-tuning large language models (LLMs), emphasizing Toubkal’s capa-
bility to handle contemporary workloads. This also underscores its strategic impor-
tance as a production HPC platform in underrepresented regions, thereby addressing 
our third research question.
Finally, to address our fourth and final research question, we compare Toubkal’s 
performance and energy efficiency with those of larger, well-established DoE sys-
tems, while also analyzing early adoption metrics to assess its impact as a scientific 
computing platform in underrepresented regions. Our findings show that Toubkal 
achieves high performance and energy efficiency across all evaluated metrics. On the 
CPU side, intra-node MPI latency reaches just 0.34 휇 s, representing a 94% reduction 
compared to Theta. On the GPU side, Toubkal-H100 delivers up to 2934 GB/s of 
sustained memory bandwidth, in line with expectations for Hopper-class architec-
tures and among the highest reported to date, while maintaining sub-microsecond 
host-to-host latency comparable to systems like Polaris and Frontier.

2  System architecture
Toubkal is designed to support a wide range of scientific workloads, from large-
scale numerical simulations to AI and data-intensive applications (see Table 4 for 
details). It combines heterogeneous Compute partitions, a scalable high-speed net-
work, and a multi-tier storage system. This section outlines the system layout, node 
configurations, interconnect design, data storage architecture, and selected scientific 
applications executed on the platform.
2.1  Compute, Himem, and GPU partitions
Toubkal features four distinct node types: general-purpose Compute nodes, high-
memory (Himem) nodes, and two generations of GPU-accelerated nodes. These 
configurations enable flexibility in workload allocation and performance tuning. 
Table 1 summarizes the key hardware characteristics of Toubkal nodes. The Com-
pute partition includes 1272 nodes based on the Dell C6420 platform. Each node 
is equipped with two Intel Xeon Platinum 8276 L processors (56 cores total) and 
192 GB of memory. This partition is optimized for parallel simulations, numerical 
solvers, and batch workloads.

2.2  Frontend and service nodes
User access is facilitated via four dedicated login nodes, each powered by dual 
Intel Xeon Platinum 8276  L processors. These nodes are designed to 
handle a variety of interactive tasks, including code development, data preprocess-
ing, job submission, and visualization. Each login node offers robust computational 
resources, ensuring efficient performance for users as they work on their projects. 
Furthermore, these nodes are directly connected to the shared parallel file system, 
allowing for seamless access to necessary data and resources. They also integrate 
with the job scheduling system (SLURM), which enables users to manage and exe-
cute their computational jobs effectively. This setup provides a user-friendly envi-
ronment that enhances productivity and streamlines workflow processes.
2.3  Interconnect architecture
Toubkal’s infrastructure is a modular, multi-tier architecture optimized for HPC and 
AI workloads. It integrates Compute, GPU, and high-memory nodes with a high-
performance storage backend and shared cluster services, connected via distinct net-
work layers for data transfer, system administration, and user access. The system 
features a hierarchical three-tier network topology, linking Compute and storage 
nodes through Top-of-Rack (ToR), aggregation, and core switches (see Fig. 1). All 
data plane switches are Mellanox, supporting 100 GbE connectivity for consistent 
bandwidth across tiers and streamlined cabling and management.
At the access layer, the Tier 3 ToR switches connect directly to Compute, GPU, 
Himem, and storage nodes within each rack, directing traffic upstream to redun-
dant Tier 2 aggregation switches (Agg1 and Agg2). These connect to Tier 1 core 
switches (Core1 and Core2), forming a robust backbone that minimizes single points 
of failure. Redundant inter-layer paths enable link aggregation and load balancing, 
enhancing fault tolerance and throughput.
A dual-rail Mellanox HDR InfiniBand fabric, with 200  Gbps links and Con-
nectX-6 adapters, provides low-latency, high-throughput communication for Com-
pute, GPU, Himem, and storage nodes. Additionally, 50 Gbps and 1 Gbps Ethernet 
networks, aggregated through a 100 Gbps uplink, support provisioning, monitoring, 
and general connectivity.

2.4  Storage architecture
The Toubkal storage subsystem integrates multiple file system technologies to sup-
port a wide range of I/O patterns and workload requirements. As shown in Fig. 2, 
storage services are connected to the InfiniBand fabric to ensure high-throughput, 
low-latency access across all Compute, Himem and GPU partitions. Three main 
storage platforms are deployed:
•	 Lustre, the primary high-performance parallel file system, provides 8  PB of 
usable capacity. It is optimized for bandwidth-intensive workloads, such as MPI-
based simulations and large-scale data staging.
•	 Isilon delivers POSIX-compliant home directories with integrated snapshotting, 
redundancy, and versioning. It ensures data protection and maintains user envi-
ronment consistency.
•	 Ceph supports internal services and containerized workflows. It provides object, 
block, and file access interfaces, enabling flexible integration with distributed 
system components.

Performance evaluation using IOR benchmarks (see Sect. 5.3) confirms that large

ever, performance tends to plateau under certain configurations, and metadata-inten-
sive workloads may suffer from latency under high concurrency. These behaviors 
highlight limitations of the current disk-based backend in handling bursty I/O and 
checkpoint-heavy scenarios.
Currently, Toubkal does not include a dedicated NVMe-based storage tier for 
I/O-intensive applications. The deployment of such a tier is under active considera-
tion, with the aim of improving support for data-intensive workflows, accelerating 
scratch I/O, and complementing the existing Lustre and Ceph infrastructure. This 
prospective addition aligns with ongoing efforts to enhance performance for large-
scale scientific and AI workloads.

3  Software ecosystem
Toubkal runs the Rocky Linux 8.9 operating system across all nodes. Job schedul-
ing and resource management are handled by SLURM [38], a workload manager 
widely adopted in HPC environments due to its scalability and hardware integration. 
Software deployment is automated using EasyBuild (v4.9.2), with Environment 
Modules providing runtime configuration. This combination enables consistent and 
reproducible environment management.
The system provides several programming environments optimized for high-
performance computing. Supported compiler toolchains include GCC​ (up to version 
13.2), Intel compilers (version 2022.2), and the NVIDIA HPC SDK (version 25.3), 
enabling development in C, C++, Fortran, and CUDA. Debugging and performance 
profiling tools include GDB, Valgrind, Intel VTune for CPU applications, 
and CUDA-GDB, NVIDIA Nsight Systems, and Nsight Compute for GPU 
workloads.
For MPI-based communication, both OpenMPI and Intel MPI are available. 
Optimized builds support both CPU and GPU workloads, with InfiniBand intercon-
nects enabled in all MPI implementations. Beyond CUDA, additional GPU pro-
gramming models are also supported, including SYCL via Intel’s DPC++ compiler, 
OpenACC through the NVIDIA HPC SDK, OpenMP with offloading capabilities, 
and OpenCL using GCC​ with the-lOpenCL flag. These options ensure portability 
and versatility for heterogeneous and accelerated computing workloads.

Toubkal leverages a range of cooling and energy management technologies for 
efficient operation. It uses a free cooling system that harnesses outside air, auto-
matically switching to water cooling and chillers when ambient temperatures 
exceed 16 °C. Located in Benguerir, which benefits from cool nights throughout 
the year, the system can extensively exploit ambient cooling. Notably, the HVAC 
infrastructure occupies only a minor portion of the data center, contributing to a 
compact layout and resulting in a measured power usage effectiveness (PUE) of

A PUE of 1.0 indicates perfect efficiency, where all consumed energy is used by the 
computing equipment. In practice, values between 1.1 and 1.4 are considered good 
for high-performance computing environments, with lower values indicating more 
efficient infrastructure.
To supplement energy efficiency, Toubkal is equipped with on-site photovol-
taic infrastructure with a peak capacity of 1 MWp. Under optimal conditions, this

4.2.2  Machine learning model for optimal GPU frequency range prediction
In this section, we present the development of a machine learning model designed 
to predict the optimal GPU frequency range for a wide variety of HPC workloads. 
As mentioned previously, the study is based on a collection of GPU benchmarks 
including matrix operations (gemm_fp16/fp32/fp64, conv1d), stencil codes 
(fdtd3d, laplace3d, hotspot3d), spectral methods (fft), copy benchmarks, 
and mixed computational workloads (cfd, gaussian, knn). The objective is to 
minimize the energy-delay product (EDP), which captures the trade-off between 
energy consumption and execution time. For each benchmark instance, the input 
features include the kernel type and a scaled representation of the problem size. The 
model predicts the frequency range that minimizes the EDP among a set of prede-
fined intervals such as 345, 345-855, 855-1350, 1350-1830, and the default 
dynamic range of onDemand 345-1830 MHz.
Preprocessing To ensure consistency and improve predictive performance, sev-
eral preprocessing steps are applied in our methodology. The initial dataset con-
tains more than 10,000 raw benchmark samples across various kernel types and 
configurations. This raw benchmark data, collected from multiple CSV files, is first 
merged, and kernel identifiers are extracted from filenames. Problem sizes, origi-
nally expressed in heterogeneous formats (e.g., 128 × 128 , 1.6M), are converted to 
numerical values and scaled using a robust quantile-based transformation per kernel 
type.
Since each configuration is tested under multiple frequency settings, we select the 
frequency that minimizes the EDP for each instance. This yields a curated dataset 
of approximately 2000 optimal configurations. The dataset is then split into training 
(80%) and validation (20%) subsets for model evaluation. This preprocessing step 
preserves intra-kernel scaling while enabling inter-kernel generalization.
Evaluation and Results We evaluate tree-based classifiers known for their strong 
performance on structured datasets: Random Forest [40], XGBoost [41], LightGBM 
[42], and CatBoost [43]. These models can naturally handle heterogeneous data 
types, provide interpretability through feature importance, and are less sensitive to 
feature scaling. Model accuracy is assessed using a held-out validation set, with the 
best-performing model (CatBoost) achieving over 92% accuracy in predicting the 
optimal frequency range. Figure 6 presents the confusion matrix of predicted versus 
true labels, showing high agreement across most frequency classes. Table 11 shows 
the classification report per class.
To quantify the impact on energy efficiency, we compute the average relative 
EDP gain for each KernelType, comparing the machine learning predictions to 
the baseline default dynamic frequency setting (345-1830 MHz). As shown in

6  Conclusion
Toubkal represents a strategic leap forward for computational research infrastructure 
in Africa. With its cutting-edge architecture, Toubkal offers computing performance 
reaching over 3.16 PFLOP/s and ranks as the most powerful supercomputer in 
Africa. Its diverse computing partitions, high-speed interconnect and advanced stor-
age system provide researchers with the tools needed to tackle complex and data-
intensive challenges across a wide range of disciplines. Toubkal has already proven 
its ability to assist researchers in advancing cutting-edge research across various 
fields, including climate modeling, bioinformatics, artificial intelligence, materials 
science, and computational fluid dynamics.
Beyond its performance, Toubkal prioritizes sustainability through innovative 
energy-efficiency strategies and the integration of renewable energy sources. Pow-
ered by on-site solar panels with a peak capacity of 1 MWp, the supercomputer can 
operate predominantly on clean energy, often reaching 100% renewable power. With 
an average power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.35 and advanced cooling systems 
that utilize free cooling and water-cooling technologies, Toubkal markedly reduces 
its environmental footprint while delivering top-tier computing performance. In 
terms of energy efficiency, Toubkal achieves 4.18 GFLOPS/W, positioning it at 
­178th place in the Green500 ranking based on the latest June 2025 listing.
We conducted experiments using H100 GPUs to leverage optimizations using the 
DVFS technology. Testing across various workload types revealed that the default 
min-max frequency range of the onDemand governor does not always optimize 
the energy-delay product (EDP). To address this, we trained a machine learning-
based model to predict the optimal frequency range based on workload characteris-
tics. Our experiments demonstrated that this ML approach significantly outperforms 
the default settings, achieving over 93% accuracy and delivering over 34% energy 
savings for memory-bound workloads, with average gains of 13% in EDP, 13% in 
energy consumption, and a 0.8% reduction in kernel time across all kernels.
To highlight Toubkal’s competitiveness on the global stage, experimental results 
presented in this paper demonstrated that Toubkal performs comparably to several 
US Department of Energy (DoE) systems. On the HPL benchmarks, we showed 
that Toubkal achieves 80 TFLOP/s, corresponding to 63% of its theoretical peak 
performance—a rate comparable to US DoE systems such as Sawtooth and Man-
zano, both of which use similar Intel Xeon Scalable CPUs and display ratios around 
62–64%. In terms of memory bandwidth, we demonstrated that Toubkal achieves 
226.05  GB/s on the CPU side, while standing out with a lower intra-node MPI 
latency (0.34 휇 s versus 0.48-−0.56 휇 s for the same systems), indicating more effi-
cient communication.
On the GPU side, our experimental results assessed that Toubkal’s performance 
excels in both internal memory access and data transfer between the CPU and GPU. Its

Our experiments and results consistently demonstrate that Toubkal maintains its 
performance levels comparable to its initial deployment four years ago, thanks to con-
tinuous software upgrades and ongoing optimizations. However, reaching this level of 
performance involves several significant challenges:
–	 Hardware maintenance is hindered by limited spare parts, long replacement times, 
firmware inconsistencies, and out-of-spec components. Managing diverse nodes 
and GPUs also requires careful driver and system configuration,
–	 Supporting diverse workloads—from HPC MPI jobs to AI pipelines—adds opera-
tional complexity, requiring frequent software updates. Network saturation, PXE 
boot issues, and inconsistent node installations further increase variability and man-
ual effort.
–	 Energy efficiency is challenged by limited solar usage due to no local storage, 
requiring seamless switching between solar and grid power via UPS to ensure sys-
tem stability,
–	 User support and training are vital as Toubkal’s growing, diverse user base needs 
accessible onboarding, troubleshooting, and documentation. Automation, standardi-
zation, and active engagement are key to reliable, scalable operation.
As Africa’s foremost supercomputer, Toubkal serves not only as a powerful compu-
tational resource but also as a crucial platform for enhancing scientific independence 
within the region, empowering local researchers, and facilitating international collab-
oration. It plays a pivotal role in building capacity among scientists and institutions, 
enabling them to address complex challenges and contribute to the global knowledge 
base. Looking ahead, future initiatives will focus on tackling the aforementioned exist-
ing challenges such as enhancing energy storage solutions to support the seamless inte-
gration of renewable energy sources, and evolving its architecture to accommodate the 
growing demands of diverse scientific communities, especially for the GPU cluster. 
We also intent to constantly update and upgrade Toubkal’s software stack and hence 
expanding access to Toubkal for a wider range of users. By doing so, Toubkal will 
continue to drive innovation and research excellence across Africa, positioning the con-
tinent as a leader in advanced scientific inquiry.

Abstract: This paper presents the architecture, performance characterization, and early sci- entific impact of Toubkal, Africa’s most powerful supercomputer (TOP500 #356, Green500 #178 as of June 2025). Designed to support high-performance computing research across disciplines, Toubkal integrates CPU, high-memory, and GPU-accel- erated nodes connected via a high-bandwidth InfiniBand fabric and powered in part by renewable energy sources. We benchmark Toubkal’s compute, memory, network, and storage subsystems using standard and reproducible tools (HPL, STREAM, IOR, OMB, HPL-MxP), reporting robust performance and energy-efficiency met- rics. The CPU partition achieves 63% of its theoretical peak, while GPU-acceler- ated HPL-MxP benchmarks on H100 nodes exceed 209 TFLOP/s per GPU. We also introduce a supervised learning model that predicts GPU frequency ranges minimiz- ing the energy-delay product (EDP) across diverse workloads. The model achieves over 92% accuracy, with average gains of 13% in EDP, 13% in energy consumption, and a 1.1% reduction in kernel time across all kernels. The paper also compares Toubkal to several US DoE systems, analyzes early user growth, and documents real-world adoption across domains including AI, bioinformatics, and material sci- ence. These results offer both a technical reference for reproducibility and a perfor- mance baseline for emerging HPC centers worldwide. Beyond presenting a system deployment, this work contributes an early blueprint for sustainable, regional super- computing infrastructure aligned with global standards.
